prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Business software subscription pricing (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Plan" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Price" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Minimum seats" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Contract" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Support" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Plan" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 75px
  col 2: header "Price › List price" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 67px
  col 3: header "Price › Billing terms" · longest unbreakable word 86px · one-line width 490px
  col 4: header "Minimum seats" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 109px
  col 5: header "Contract" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 123px
  col 6: header "Support" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 195px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 707px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 706px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"A plan-comparison price sheet: the reader first identifies a plan, then reads across to see what it costs, what the billing commitment is, and what operational constraints (seats, contract, support) come with it.","reading":"Mostly row-wise: the eye anchors on the Plan name, jumps to the Price block (list price then the billing sentence that explains it), then continues right to the short fact columns (seats, contract, support) which are scanned vertically for comparison between plans. Column 3 is prose, not a value; columns 2/4/5/6 are short comparable facts.","groups":["cols 1 alone — row identity, the entry point for every scan","cols 2–3 — one merged 'Price' header; the number and its terms must be adjacent and read together","cols 4–6 — short constraint/support facts of equal role, read as a small comparable block","col 2 vs cols 4–6 — numeric/short tokens that benefit from tight, uniform widths"],"keep_intact":["Plan names, especially 'Enterprise' (75px, must not break)","'List price' and 'Billing terms' as word units (no mid-word breaks)","'Minimum seats', 'Contract', 'Support' as word units in the header","dollar amounts ($12, $45) and figures like 250+ in the billing text","'12-month', '40%' tokens inside billing text"],"may_wrap":["Billing terms sentence in col 3 (longest, 490px one-line — the natural place to absorb height)","'List price' header over two lines","'Minimum seats' header over two lines","Support descriptions in col 6","Contract wording in col 5"]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r0A: widths [96, 58, 281, 87, 84, 100] · table 707×593px · row heights [36, 60, 83, 83, 83, 83, 83, 83] · column headers wrapped 2/7 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0B: widths [100, 70, 200, 115, 110, 111] · table 707×593px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 83, 83, 83, 83, 106] · column headers wrapped 2/7 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0C: widths [110, 62, 160, 130, 120, 124] · table 707×733px · row heights [36, 60, 83, 83, 106, 129, 106, 129] · column headers wrapped 1/7 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}

log.raw: {"critique":[{"design":"r0A","good":"Plan at 96px keeps 'Enterprise' on one line, and the 281px billing column reads comfortably in 2 lines for every plan, so the price sentence never fragments. The three fact columns are clearly a block on the right.","problems":"The table is uniformly 83px per body row — every row is as tall as its worst cell, so short facts like '1' or 'Annual only' sit in vast vertical space. 'List price' is squeezed to two stacked lines in a 58px column, 'Monthly or annual' breaks over three lines, and Support breaks over three to four lines. Overall the table is bloated at 593px for content that mostly needs two lines.","cause":"58px in col 2 leaves exactly 37px of text — the bare minimum for 'price', so the header cannot sit on one line; 84px in col 5 (63px text) cannot hold 'Monthly or annual' (123px) on one line and forces 3 lines; 100px in col 6 (79px text) forces 3–4 lines in Support. Meanwhile 281px in col 3 is more than the billing text needs (2 lines everywhere), so ~60px of slack is wasted on the one column that could have absorbed nothing more."},{"design":"r0B","good":"The most balanced of the three: reallocating width from billing to the fact columns drops the tallest cell from 4–5 lines to 4 only in the worst row, 'Minimum seats' and 'Contract' now read cleanly in two lines, and Plan at 100px is safe. Tests whether giving the numeric column the tightest defensible width and spending the savings on billing produces the shortest table without splitting any word."}]}
